title: Bose’s Bestselling QuietComfort Headphones Are More Than Half Off for Amazon Prime Big Deals Day
description:

body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	If you’ve been holding out for a pair of Bose noise-cancelling headphones, Amazon’s fall Prime event has brought one of the brand’s most popular pairs down to a much more accesible price.

	The Bose QuietComfort Headphones are on sale for $169 during Prime Big Deal Days, down $130 from their $359 list price. That works out to roughly 53% off the over-ear headphones, with the deal currently available on select colors, including the limited-edition Petal Pink model.


		

						
			
	

	
					
		

										LIMITED-EDITION						

					Bose QuietComfort Headphones in Petal Pink		

		
	

	The QuietComforts have long been Bose’s more accessible alternative to its flagship Ultra headphones, delivering the feature the company is best known for — powerful active noise cancellation — without pushing into the $400-plus territory of its top-of-the-line models. The headphones feature both Quiet Mode, which maximizes noise cancellation, and Aware Mode, which lets outside sound back in when you need to stay tuned into your surroundings. Users can also create custom listening modes and adjust bass, midrange and treble through the Bose app.

	Battery life clocks in at up to 24 hours on a full charge, while a 15-minute quick charge provides up to 2.5 additional hours of listening. Plush ear cushions and a padded over-ear design are built for longer listening sessions, and Bluetooth multipoint lets you stay connected to two devices — handy for bouncing between a laptop and phone without repeatedly pairing and unpairing. An included audio cable also means you can keep listening when Bluetooth isn’t an option, including through an airplane’s in-flight entertainment system.

	There is one thing worth keeping in mind before adding them to your cart: these are the original QuietComfort Headphones released in 2023, rather than Bose’s newly released second-generation model (which are also nearly 20% off for Prime Big Deals Day). Bose introduced the QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) in August, keeping the $359 starting price while adding a refreshed design, Bluetooth 5.4, USB-C audio and the company’s Immersive Audio technology. But if you’re primarily after Bose’s noise cancellation, comfort and wireless listening — and don’t need the newest spatial-audio bells and whistles — knocking $130 off the previous generation makes the older pair considerably easier to recommend.


		

	

	
					
		

					Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen)		

			
							
	$369


	$449


	18% off

															
	
		
	

	The deal arrives as part of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days 2026, the retailer’s annual fall counterpart to Prime Day. This year’s sale runs Oct. 6 through Oct. 7, beginning at 12:01 a.m. PDT Tuesday and ending at 11:59 p.m. PDT Wednesday. Amazon says the 48-hour event spans more than 35 categories, including electronics, fashion, beauty, home, toys and holiday gifts, with limited-time “Today’s Big Deals” dropping three times a day at midnight, 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. PDT.

	The October event follows Amazon’s main Prime Day sale, which expanded to four days in 2026 and ran from June 23 through June 26. Like Prime Day, most Prime Big Deal Days offers are reserved for Amazon Prime subscribers; membership currently costs $14.99 per month or $139 annually, and eligible new members can access the sale through a 30-day free trial.

title: France Boosts Oscar Campaign Support as Industry Sounds Alarm Over Declining Exports
description:
France’s National Film Board (CNC) has unveiled a new strategy to boost the profile of French movies and talent navigating the Oscar race. 

	Unveil
body:
France’s National Film Board (CNC) has unveiled a new strategy to boost the profile of French movies and talent navigating the Oscar race. 

	Unveiled during a conference on film and TV exports held at the CNC on Monday, the new strategy will see the government-back organization double the financial aid granted to campaigns. The CNC has also appointed Sébastien Cauchon as its “Academy Awards” liaison. Under this newly created role, Cauchon will spearhead the campaign for “Minotaur.” 
	

	The country has not won the international feature prize since Régis Wargnier’s “Indochine” took the honor in 1993, despite frequent nominations in that category. 


	The exec, who recently founded the Paris-based consultancy Cinema Collectors, comes into the role fresh off the Oscar-winning campaign forn Natalie Musteata and Alexandre Singh’s “Two People Exchanging Saliva.” His other awards work includes serving as a consultant and international publicist on Mubi’s campaign for Coralie Fargeat’s “The Substance,” as well as a longstanding collaboration with Florian Zeller that included “The Father,” which won two Oscars. 

	Speaking at Monday’s conference, Cauchon said France has been relatively slow to embrace the kind of specialized awards strategy. 

	“An awards strategist is a profession that isn’t very widespread in France, or even in Europe,” Cauchon said, describing the job as combining publicity, marketing and influence to make sure films and talent are seen by Academy members and stay on voters’ radar throughout the race.

	For the CNC, the broader goal is also to move beyond France’s traditional focus on the international feature category and better coordinate campaigns across directing, acting, screenplay and craft categories.
	

	“In France, we sometimes focus a lot on the best international film category,” Cauchon said. “But we have such a diversity of productions and talent that we’re represented much more broadly across all the categories.” Case in point, many French movies that thrived in the awards season in recent years, from Coralie Fargeat’s “The Substance” to Florian Zeller’s “The Father,” Gints Zilbalodis’s “Flow, and Justine Triet’s “Anatomy of a Fall,” did not represent France in the Oscar race. 

	This year, Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Cannes Grand Prize winner “Minotaur” (Mubi) will represent France, but other films that were shortlisted by the French committee could turn up in nominations, notably Marine Atlan’s Cannes Critics Week winner “La Gradiva” (1 2 Special), Louis Clichy’s animated feature “Iron Boy” (SPC) which won a prize at Cannes’ Un Certain Regard, and Antonin Baudry’s “De Gaulle” (Samuel Goldwyn Films). There’s also Lea Seydoux with two movies, “The Unknown” by Arthur Harari (Neon), and “Gentle Monster” by Marie Kreutzer (Netflix).

	The CNC’s new approach will aim at pooling resources earlier in the process and work alongside U.S. distributors. 

	That tension between France’s cultural standing and the increasingly competitive global marketplace ran through Monday’s conference, where French film and TV figures warned that the country’s international position can no longer be taken for granted.

	CNC president Gaëtan Bruel pointed out France remained in 2025 the third most represented country after the U.S. and U.K. in terms of content broadcast on linear TV worldwide, but the country has so far failed to achieve the same level of success on streaming platforms.

	“We’ve spent years — rightly — celebrating the fact that we fill the top 100 fiction rankings on television, without seeing that we were losing the streaming battle,” Bruel said. He noted the contrasting performances of countries such as Spain and South Korea, where local programming commands a much larger share of streaming consumption.

	“To put it clearly, Spanish Netflix subscribers watch Spanish series first, ahead of American ones,” Bruel said. “French subscribers watch American series first, and then more Spanish and Korean series than French ones.”
	

	Speaking of Korea and Spain, he said there were “smaller markets that were forced to think internationally from the outset because their domestic industries could not sustain production on their own.” 

	France, on the other hand, has relied on its own market fir a long time thanks to its “unusually robust internal system of financing, production and distribution.”

	“That’s an immense strength and there is obviously no question of abandoning it. But I think that strength explains why we have had less need than others to think internationally from the very beginning of projects. That is what now has to evolve, because the world has changed,” Bruel said. 

	UniFrance president Gilles Pélisson similarly warned that the rise of tech giants, streaming platforms and AI had fundamentally reshaped the balance of power facing European content producers.

	“The tech giants, which are now publishers — more or less, depending on the company — are taking power,” Pélisson said. “And all of this is happening in the context of the evolution of AI, which is impacting absolutely every sector.”

	Pélisson, who works alongside Unifrance’s well respected managing director Daniel Elstner, called for France to revamp export support schemes, including funds for film, television and shorts, as well as assistance for foreign distributors who release French works.

	“We have to think more broadly than our French territory,” he said. “Foreign distributors are obviously allies. How do we continue supporting them? We probably need to think about creating new forms of support.”

	For Pélisson, one of the industry’s most pressing battles is over data. Streamers’ reluctance to share detailed viewing data, he argued, is directly tied to the economic value of the works they carry.

	“Data today is the underlying key to the value of works. And that’s why, strangely enough, the platforms have so much difficulty sharing data. Of course they do — it’s exactly what determines the value of our works and the value of your works.”

	French sales agents, meanwhile, said France already boasts one of the strongest networks of international sellers in the world who are handling major non-French festival titles, for instance MK2 Films with “Minotaur,” Goodfellas with “La Bola Negra” and “Fjord,” and Charades with “Club Kid.” 
	

	“We have in France the best, densest and most effective export network. Producers from all over the world come to France to have their films sold,” said Pierre Mazars, co-founder of Charades which sold “Club Kid” to A24 at Cannes, among other films. 

	Yet, Mazars, who also co-presides over the French exporters association ADEF, warned that those companies need to be incentivized take risks on French movies. 

	“The reality, and we have to say it, is that for exporters it is often more attractive within the ecosystem to sell a foreign film than a French film. The system isn’t sufficiently incentivizing for us to sell French films,” Mazars.

	French sellers, he said, are increasingly being asked to put up sizable minimum guarantees while international competitors, such as in the U.K., are introducing schemes aimed at reducing those risks.

	Mazars also called on France to explore ways of attracting private equity into film financing, citing MK2’s partnership with IPR.VC, a Helsinki and London-based fund manager, as one possible model.

	“I think there is work to be done between exporters, the CNC and perhaps Bpifrance to bring private equity funds into French cinema. We all know the difficulties producers have financing their films,“ he said. 

	Clara Flageollet Schmit, sales manager at SND and ADEF’s co-president, said the role of international sales agents themselves has changed dramatically as they take on more financial exposure at ever earlier stages of production.

	“We’re no longer simply intermediaries. Today we’re real financiers of cinema, and particularly French cinema. We’re getting involved earlier and earlier in projects, sometimes from the development stage,” she said. “We also participate in casting, and we’re putting up increasingly substantial minimum guarantees, often on first and second films.”

	While preliminary UniFrance figures suggest French films should reach around 42.5 million admissions and €272 million in international box office revenue in 2025, Flageollet Schmit said the sector remains roughly 26% below pre-pandemic levels while the cost of doing business has soared.

	“It’s becoming increasingly complicated to accompany films abroad, particularly French films, where we’re investing more and more,” she said. “Supporting risk means supporting investment, and supporting investment means supporting international growth.”

title: How David Ellison Won the Battle: Timeline of Paramount’s Rocky Road to Acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery
description: It’s been a hell of a ride. David Ellison’s quest to control two iconic Hollywood studios has finally been completed — added a rollicking new chapte
body:
It’s been a hell of a ride. David Ellison’s quest to control two iconic Hollywood studios has finally been completed — added a rollicking new chapter to the storied recent history of Hollywood megamergers.

	On the morning of Tuesday, Oct. 6, the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger officially closed. The new company, Skydance Corp., brings together film and TV assets into one big company, which is weighed down by some $80 billion in debt.The storyline’s arc features appearances by such colorful subjects as President Donald Trump, 12 blue-state attorneys general, Netflix, Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds, the Block the Merger coalition, Mark Ruffalo, David Zaslav and so much more. Here’s a timeline of how it all happened.
	

	
		2025	

	Aug. 7, 2025: Skydance Media completes its $8 billion acquisition of Paramount Global after a tumultuous yearlong closing process.




	

					David Zaslav, CEO and President of Warner Bros. Discovery
									Getty Images
	



	September 2025: First rumblings surface of David Ellison’s overtures to David Zaslav and the Warner Bros. Discovery board of directors

	Oct. 21, 2025: Warner Bros. Discovery formally initiates sale process “in light of unsolicited interest” the company has received from “multiple parties.”

	November 2025: Netflix, Comcast and Skydance Media submit offers for all or portions of Warner Bros. Discovery.



	

									Getty Images
	



	Dec. 5, 2025: Netflix wins the auction process as Warner Bros. Discovery announces it has set an $82.7 billion cash and stock acquisition agreement to sell Warner Bros. and HBO (but not CNN, TNT and other cable channels) to the streaming giant.

	Dec. 8, 2025: Paramount Skydance ups the ante, launching a tender offer for Warner Bros. Discovery shares and a campaign to convince WBD shareholders to back its bid. “Our proposal is superior to Netflix’s in every dimension,” David Ellison tells Wall Street analysts on a conference call.

	Dec. 17, 2025: Warner Bros. Discovery board unanimously recommends shareholders reject Paramount’s tender offer.
	

	Dec. 22, 2025: Warner Bros. Discovery receives amended tender offer from Paramount

	
		2026	

	Jan. 7: WBD board unanimously recommends shareholders reject latest Paramount tender offer.

	Jan. 20: Netflix agrees to revise its deal to acquire Warner Bros. and HBO to all cash, in a bid to counter the pressure from Paramount’s repeated offers.

	Feb. 10: Paramount adds a “ticking fee” to its offer that promises to pay WBD shareholders $650 million per quarter that the transaction is not closed after Dec. 31, 2026.

	Feb. 17: WBD sets March 20 for special meeting of shareholders to vote on Netflix transaction. At the same time, WBD opens a 10-day negotiating window with Paramount to address the latest offer.

	Feb. 24: WBD confirms receipt of a new offer from Paramount Skydance. Later that day WBD issues a statement acknowledging that it could “reasonably be expected to lead to a ‘Company Superior Proposal’” as spelled out in its Netflix sale agreement.



	

					Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos
									Getty Images
	



	Feb. 26: Netflix formally bows out of the WBD chase, declining to match the higher Paramount offer. “The deal is no longer financially attractive,” Netflix told investors. Rob Bonta, California’s Attorney General, gives the first indication of the antitrust suit to come by promising to begin a “vigorous review” of the transaction.

	Feb. 27: Paramount formally seals its $110 billion all-cash agreement to acquire all of Warner Bros. Discovery. The final terms amend the ticking fee to kick in as of Oct. 1.

	April 13: A group of 1,000 industry creatives sign the open letter calling on officials to “Block the Merger,” including Ben Stiller, Kristen Stewart, Joaquin Phoenix, Adam McKay, Alan Cumming, Alyssa Milano, Boots Riley, Bryan Cranston, Cynthia Nixon, Damon Lindelof, David Fincher and Denis Villeneuve. Ten days later it had 4,000 signatures.

	April 16: AMC Theatres CEO Adam Aron endorses the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger on the cusp of the CinemaCon gathering in Las Vegas.

	April 23: WBD shareholders vote to approve the sale to Paramount.



	

					Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman and Chairman of the Saudi Public Investment Fund, an investor in the combined Warner Bros. and Paramount Studios
									Getty Images
	



	April 27: Paramount discloses in a regulatory filing that about 38.5% of the equity in the new company will be held by the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.
	

	June 12: The Justice Department closes its investigation into the merger, without imposing any conditions or divestitures.



	

					California Attorney General Rob Bonta 
									Getty Images
	



	July 13: Twelve state attorneys general — including California’s Rob Bonta and New York’s Leticia James — file suit to block the Paramount-WBD transaction on antitrust grounds.

	July 14: The Writers Guild of America sues to block the merger on antitrust grounds.

	July 20: A federal judge puts a 14-day hold on the merger as the states seek a temporary injunction.

	July 22: European Commission approves the transaction.



	

					The SAG-AFTRA building in Los Angeles
									Variety via Getty Images
	



	July 27: SAG-AFTRA issues a statement against the merger, calling for it to be blocked unless “enforceable safeguards” are implemented.

	July 29: Regal Cinemas CEO Eduardo Acuna announces its support of merger

	July 31: Paramount asks for a November start date for the states’ antitrust trial. The states and the WGA seek an April 2027 start date.

	Aug. 4: Judge sets March 2, 2027, as the start date for states’ antitrust trial.



	

									Getty Images
	



	Aug. 5: David Ellison tells senior Paramount execs that he will move the company out of California as of Oct. 1 if the state AGs don’t drop their antitrust lawsuit aimed at blocking the merger.

	Aug. 6: Paramount secures approval from U.K. Competition and Markets Authority.

	Aug. 12: The Directors Guild of America and IATSE sent a letter to California attorney general Rob Bonta and David Ellison calling on them to reach a settlement or jointly push for a faster timeline for the trial, for the sake of both studios. The letter outlines 10 conditions that could help alleviate antitrust concerns.

	Aug. 14: Mexico clears the transaction.

	Aug. 17: Paramount asks the court to order the states to put up a $1.88 billion bond to cover the costs of the ticking fee it will owe Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders if Paramount prevails in the lawsuit.

	Aug. 18: Cinemark exhibition chain announces its support for the merger.



	

					Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass 
									Variety via Getty Images
	



	Aug. 20: Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass urges Rob Bonta to settle with Paramount.
	

	Aug. 21: David Ellison holds private meeting with state AGs to agree on date for settlement talks.

	Aug. 23: Rob Bonta cancels planned Aug. 24 meeting for settlement talks after word of the meeting leaks to media outlets.

	Sept. 11: Paramount argues in a motion that the states’ case is “a series of attempted shortcuts and assumptions that collapse under scrutiny.”



	

					Jessica J. González at Block the Merger #NoConcessions Action Rally held at Paramount Pictures Studio on September 03, 2026 
									Variety via Getty Images
	



	Sept. 12: Los Angeles Economic Development Corporation reports that the loss of Paramount from California would cost the state $1 billion-$2 billion in economic output over four years.

	Sept. 15: Justice Department sides with Paramount on the fight over the $1.88 billion bond.

	Sept. 17: FCC approves up to 49.5% foreign ownership in Paramount Skydance deal in connection with CBS O&O stations.



	

					Sunrise Coigney and Mark Ruffalo at the Emmy Awards on September 14, 2026
									Variety via Getty Images
	



	Sept. 19: Actor Mark Ruffalo warns Rob Bonta “Don’t You Dare Settle” the states’ case via social media.

	Sept. 21: Paramount announces settlement with 12 state attorneys general that includes numerous stipulations but no structural remedies.

	Sept. 24: David Ellison attend President Donald Trump’s state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping; Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín questions the sides on the settlement

	Sept. 25: Paramount Skydance says it will move its Class B common stock shares from the Nasdaq index to the New York Stock Exchange as of Oct. 5-6.

	Sept. 30: Paramount sets Oct. 6 as closing date for the transaction after a federal judge approves the states’ antitrust settlement agreement. David Ellison surprises Hollywood by recruiting Mattel leader Ynon Kreiz to become co-CEO of the enlarged company.

	Oct. 2: David Ellison announces the new name of the company: Skydance Corp., a nod to the name of the film production firm he founded in 2006.  

	Oct. 5: Ellison unveils the new leadership team for Skydance, which he will lead alongside Kreiz. The film business will be headed by Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, previously co-chairs of Paramount Pictures, and James Gunn and Peter Safran will continue as co-heads of DC Studios. George Cheeks, previously chair of TV media at Paramount Skydance, is co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance TV. Casey Bloys, who has headed up HBO and HBO Max, will become co-chair and chief content officer, Skydance DTC streaming. Warner Bros. Discovery exec JB Perrette is co-chair and chief business officer of both Skydance TV and Skydance DTC. Mark Thompson will continue to run CNN as CEO.

	Oct. 6: The merger officially closes, creating Skydance Corp. WBD shares cease trading on Nasdaq, and the new company’s shares begin trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol “SKYD.”

schema.headline: How David Ellison Won the Battle: Timeline of Paramount’s Rocky Road to Acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery

title: London Film Festival Director on Why the Event Has Become Awards Season’s Unofficial Starter Gun: ‘The Whole World Is Here’
description: With its positioning in October after the likes of Berlin, Cannes, Venice, Toronto and Telluride have helped anoint most of the year’s buzziest and
body:
With its positioning in October after the likes of Berlin, Cannes, Venice, Toronto and Telluride have helped anoint most of the year’s buzziest and most talked about films, the BFI London Film Festival has long been an event where many of these films come together in one place for the first time. This year’s LFF is no exception, kicking off on Oct. 7 with the European premiere of “Elsinore” and a lineup including the likes of “Club Kid,” “Wild Horse Nine,” “The Debut,” “Ink,” “La Bola Negra,” “Primetime,” “Tender Loving Care” and many, many more.
	

	But over the last few years, the LFF has also risen to become one of the most important first stops in awards season. For many, it’s now effectively the unofficial starter gun for the race, at least from an international perspective. Because alongside 12 days of public-facing screenings, for voters there’s now also wall-to-wall FYC screenings, tastemaker events, Q&As and cocktails. Filmmakers and stars who would previously turn up solely for their premiere are now given tightly-packed, days-long schedules in which they’re ferried between events to talk about their work and pose for selfies.


	It’s something that festival director Kristy Matheson is well aware of, and says the festival’s increasingly important awards status just as the season kicks into gear is something that has been long in the works.

	“I feel like where the festival is positioned now is really a testament to the former directors of the festival and how they really worked very hard to put this particular stop in the calendar on the map for people,” she says. “Obviously, there’s an enormous amount of awards voters who who are here in the U.K., but also the U.K. is a really important market for film releases.”
	

	Matheson isn’t wrong about voters, who in the weeks before the festival have seen their inboxes stack up with invites to special events. 

	According to figures released last year, London had the largest concentration of AMPAS voters outside of the U.S, with some 800 — 7% of the total — residing in the U.K. Across Europe, the number more than doubles to 1,750 or 15%, with many expected to fly in for the festival. And these are figures that are only rising as the Academy expands its global outreach.

	For Matheson, alongside the festival’s public events, having all the extra activity around the side “feels like a vote of confidence” in both the LFF and its selection of films. 

	“We don’t play films that we don’t really believe in or films where we don’t think we can help them find their perfect audience,” she says. “But it’s enormously satisfying that it feels like there is a vote of confidence from the industry in the festival.”

	The awards focus is something that the festival has also been able to capitalize on itself with its scheduling, not least with its Screen Talks. This year sees arguably its biggest crop of names to date, with Andrew Scott, Cynthia Erivo, Sophia Coppola, Javier Bardem, Brad Bird, John Malkovich, Ava DuVernay, Naomi Ackie, Danny Boyle, Robert Eggers and James Gray sitting down for hour-long discussions. Several of these are already being touted as likely Oscar nominees.

	“Most of them of here with a film,” says Matheson of the Screen Talk stars, who adds that, unlike the standard FYC Q&As about a specific title, these talks are often more of a career conversation, something generally more preferable for talent.

	Of course, there another key factor as to why LFF has become awards season’s international launch pad: London itself. 

	It’s a capital that has long held the position as one of the world’s biggest filmmaking hubs, a status underlined with each and every major Hollywood tentpole that shoots there (the film many expect may become the most successful of all time, “Avengers: Doomsday,” filmed primarily in Pinewood). As Matheson notes, that means that much of the industry either lives in the city or has, at some point, probably worked in it. 

	“The whole world is here — it’s the epicenter of culture,” she says. “And, for filmmakers, they’re bringing their films to an audience that is incredibly savvy.”

schema.headline: London Film Festival Director on Why the Event Has Become Awards Season’s Unofficial Starter Gun: ‘The Whole World Is Here’

title: ‘All’s Fair’ Season 2 to Launch From Rome Film Festival With Kim Kardashian, Naomi Watts, Niecy Nash-Betts and Sarah Paulson Attending
description: The second season of Ryan Murphy’s legal drama “All’s Fair” is set to have its world premiere at the upcoming Rome Film Festival with stars Kim Kard
body:
The second season of Ryan Murphy’s legal drama “All’s Fair” is set to have its world premiere at the upcoming Rome Film Festival with stars Kim Kardashian, Naomi Watts, Niecy Nash-Betts and Sarah Paulson in tow.

	The first episode of Season 2 of the divisive show — which follows a team of female divorce attorneys who leave a male-dominated firm to start their own powerhouse practice — will bow on the evening of Oct. 24 in the Eternal City’s Auditorium Parco della Musica as part of the festival’s Freestyle section.
	

	“All’s Fair” Season 2 will subsequently debut at a still unspecified November date exclusively on Disney+ in Italy and internationally, and on Hulu in the United States.


	The Ryan Murphy series debuted on Nov. 4, 2025, and quickly became a camp classic despite being despised by critics. It was also a ratings hit, launching at No. 1 on the Hulu viewership chart and becoming the streamer’s biggest original scripted series premiere in three years (based on the first three days of streaming).

	In the new installment, the lawyers at Grant, Ronson & Greene “return for a new season of scandals, secrets and stilettos,” according to a provided synopsis. “As new alliances form and friendships are put to the test, a shocking revelation threatens the very existence of the firm.”

	Alongside Kardashian, Watts, Nash-Betts and Paulson, the series stars Teyana Taylor, Matthew Noszka and Glenn Close, who all one-up each other with deliriously absurd lines of dialogue. (There’s talk of “piggly-wiggly titties” and “blowing a priest with chlamydia,” but Paulson takes the cake, perhaps, with “see you in court, cuntburger.”)
	

	“All’s Fair” is produced by 20th Television in association with Ryan Murphy, who also directs. Executive producers include Jon Robin Baitz, Joe Baken, Jamie Pachino, Lyn Greene and Richard Levine, alongside Kardashian, Close, Watts, Nash-Betts and Paulson. Anthony Hemingway also executive produces and directs. Kris Jenner, Eric Kovtun, Scott Robertson and Nissa Diederich also executive produce.

	The Rome Film Festival will run Oct. 13-25.

schema.headline: ‘All’s Fair’ Season 2 to Launch From Rome Film Festival With Kim Kardashian, Naomi Watts, Niecy Nash-Betts and Sarah Paulson Attending

title: LL Cool J Returns to the Big Apple In CBS’ Solid and Steady ‘NCIS: New York’: TV Review
description: Three years after “NCIS: Los Angeles” wrapped its 14-season run, LL Cool J has returned to the franchise as Senior Special Agent Sam Hanna in CBS’ n
body:
Three years after “NCIS: Los Angeles” wrapped its 14-season run, LL Cool J has returned to the franchise as Senior Special Agent Sam Hanna in CBS’ new “NCIS” spinoff, “NCIS: New York.” Created by R. Scott Gemmill — also the creator of “The Pitt” — the series follows Sam, who returns to his hometown after years working in the field across the globe. Though Sam is initially in New York only for one case, he finds himself drawn to the city and to a new team who are ready to defend one of the world’s most vital ports. Though critics were just given the pilot for review, the episode works fine as a new extension of one of CBS’ longest-running franchises.
	
	The 20-episode season opens nearly 7,000 miles away from the Big Apple. Sam, who speaks Arabic fluently and whose specialties brought him to the Middle East, is working in Dubai. However, he is distracted by the repeated rings of his cellphone. An old friend, a Navy Reservist, has called him several times and left numerous voicemails. Sam notes the calls, but he keeps focusing on his case. Unfortunately, by the time he returns his friend’s phone call, the man is lying dead on a bench in Central Park.Back stateside, Sam finds himself at the Naval Criminal Investigative Service’s New York office at the Brooklyn Navy Yard. After convincing Assistant Special Agent-in-Charge Robyn Wells (Jennifer Beals) to let him investigate what happened to his friend, Robyn partners Sam with Nick Schaeffer (Scott Caan, playing a different role from his “Hawaii Five-O” character, who’d appeared on “NCIS: Los Angeles in a crossover episode). Nick is an agent with a devil-may-care attitude, who shares Sam’s love of NYC. Rounding out the New York field office are Special Agent Addison “Addy” Ross (Jacqueline Byers), Special Agent Wyatt Sellers (Shane Harper) and Sean Sullivan (Devin Druid), a young, ill-mannered techie who’s stuck working for NCIS only because he was caught hacking the police pension fund.“NCIS: New York” works like a well-oiled machine. Sam and Nick’s first case involves murder, a love scam, kidnapping and a massive shootout. Viewers get only glimmers of the characters’ personalities and backgrounds, but the show offers enough detail and texture to understand how Season 1 might unfold. LL Cool J’s Sam and Caan’s Nick have great chemistry and work well as a buddy-comedy duo rather than a dark, overserious pair, which adds levity to the series. Despite some corny jokes that mostly play on the two men’s height difference, their banter is all in good fun and will undoubtedly endear itself to long-time fans of the “NCIS” universe.New York City also plays a major role in “NCIS: New York.” While trying to solve the mystery of the Navy Reservist’s death, Sam and the team journey across town, from Brooklyn to Queens and even the Diamond District in Midtown. Beyond the repartee between Nick and Sam, Addy and Wyatt share a sibling-like relationship that could turn into something more, especially since Wyatt is nursing a broken heart following the sudden end of his engagement. Moreover, “NCIS” fans will certainly be interested to see what kind of bond and connection Sam and Robyn could form, even as he still mourns his late wife.“NCIS: New York” is a solid spinoff. Though the show (thus far) doesn’t necessarily elevate the franchise, it has all the components that have made it a staple of network television for the last two decades. With a beloved character in Sam and some brand-new faces entering the scene, the show is steady, intriguing and will likely go the distance.

	“NCIS: New York” debuts Oct. 6 on CBS, with the remaining episodes airing weekly on Tuesdays.

title: AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Sets First Trailer for December Theatrical Run, Plans Oscar Bid for Best Animated Feature
description:
It’ll take a bit longer for the first AI-generated film to make it to theaters — because it’s gunning for an Oscar.

	The AI studio Fable has shifte
body:
It’ll take a bit longer for the first AI-generated film to make it to theaters — because it’s gunning for an Oscar.

	The AI studio Fable has shifted the U.S. release of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” the collection of four anthology shorts by the AI-focused YouTuber Gossip Goblin (né Zack London), from Oct. 30 to Dec. 4. While Fable has not yet disclosed a distributor for the film, the film’s trailer will make its debut in theaters on Friday, and its poster will spread across U.S. multiplexes.
	

	Fable and London revealed their ambitious plans for a theatrical rollout in July, hoping to follow the path laid by YouTubers-turned-filmmakers Kane Parsons and Mark Fischbach, or Markiplier, who leveraged their respective YouTube followings to box office successes in “Backrooms” ($401 million) and “Iron Lung” ($51.2 million). Its story — which lies within the “second cycle of humanity” within the Gossip Goblin universe’s “13 cycles” and aims to satirize society’s relationship with AI — traces the fallout of humanity besting earthly limitations like death and memory through technology and how it grapples with humanity as a result.


	But the roughly monthlong delay comes with an ulterior motive: a bid to get the project closer to the traditional Oscar campaign season. Fable plans to submit the film for consideration in the best animated feature category for the upcoming Oscars, testing both the Academy’s hesitation toward publicly AI-powered films and whether AI-generated projects can stand among films generally regarded as the year’s best in cinema. 
	

	The campaign will also include advanced screenings for Academy voters, pre-release screenings for critics and a billboard advertising campaign across Los Angeles next month, all to celebrate what Fable CEO Edward Saatchi claims is “a seminal, historic moment in animation.” 

	“For 5 years, the question has been when will an AI film win an Oscar? Gods Don’t Give Gifts is the first that has a shot at a nomination and then it’s all to play for,” Saatchi said in a statement. “We feel it could be this generation’s Toy Story – the fact that this generation’s Toy Story is a dark, satirical, bold statement on all 2026’s fears about AI and our species’ future is an appropriate commentary on the questions we are all confronting as a society.”

	London describes the anthology in a statement as “part speculation, part critique” and hopes audiences can “take a premise seriously, follow its emotional consequences, and let the results be strange, funny, grotesque, and sad.”

	“I made these films with AI, which some people find ironic,” he said. “But using a medium to interrogate that medium is one of the oldest moves in art; I may just be early to do it with AI. But what AI actually gave me is the ability to transmit stories onto a screen, with minimal filters, intervention, committees or constraints. Its enabled myself and a small talented team to envision an extravagant world, down to its smallest prop, and bring it to life with extraordinary fidelity – from jaw-dropping visuals of leviathans and space ships and talking apes, down to the scuffed up sneakers on a background extra.”

	“Gods Don’t Give Gifts” will represent the biggest test of whether the Academy is willing to accept wholesale AI-generated films since its May ban on AI actors or AI-assisted scripts. But generally, according to its published eligibility rules, AI tools “neither help nor harm the chances of achieving a nomination” and the relevant Academy branches will “judge the achievement, taking into account the degree to which a human was at the heart of the creative authorship when choosing which movie to award.” 

	“If questions arise regarding the aforementioned use of Generative Artificial Intelligence, the Academy reserves the right to request more information about the nature of the use and human authorship,” the rules state.
	

	The film’s violence, and “R” rating from the Motion Picture Association, may also serve as a barrier. The first R-rated film nominated for best animated feature was Charlie Kaufman’s 2015 stop-motion picture “Anomalisa.”

title: Paramount-Warner Bros. $111 Billion Merger Officially Closes: ‘Today Is a Historic Day, Not Just for Skydance but for Our Entire Industry,’ David Ellison Says
description: It’s official: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery are now a single company — joined together as Skydance Corp., led by chairman and CEO David Elli
body:
It’s official: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery are now a single company — joined together as Skydance Corp., led by chairman and CEO David Ellison.

	The deal, valued at $111 billion including the assumption of WBD debt, brings together two major studios, TV networks including CBS, CNN, Comedy Central, MTV and TBS, and streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max. The new Skydance will have annual revenue of nearly $70 billion, the company said — but it also will have to wrestle with $80 billion in net debt.
	

	The closing of the deal comes a little more than a year after Ellison’s Paramount Skydance (created in 2025 after his Skydance Media bought Paramount Global) first launched his bid for Warner Bros. Discovery. The 43-year-old Ellison encountered numerous obstacles on the way there — including a rival Netflix deal for WB assets and an antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 Democratic attorneys general — but has now prevailed in sealing the deal.


	The Ellison family — with the multibillion-dollar backing of Larry Ellison, David’s tech-mogul father — holds the largest equity stake in Skydance. The Ellisons and investment firm RedBird Capital Partners together are the sole holders of Paramount Class A common stock, including 100% of the combined company’s voting shares.

	RELATED: Skydance Blasts Off: Can David Ellison Make Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Fly?

	Skydance Class B shares will begin trading Tuesday on the New York Stock Exchange under the new ticker symbol “SKYD.” Under the terms of the merger, Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders received an amount in cash equal to $31.01666668 per share. WBD shares have ceased trading on Nasdaq effective Tuesday.
	

	“Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said in a statement. 

	The CEO continued: “From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality…. Our focus now turns to the future: building a company that empowers creatives, entertains audiences and rewards shareholders.”

	The merger creating Skydance was funded with $47 billion of investment in Class B common stock, led by Larry Ellison, RedBird Capital Partners, LionTree, and the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. That equity investment was priced at $12 per share. Debt financing for the transaction was led by Bank of America, Citigroup and Apollo Global Management.

	Ellison has hired Ynon Kreiz, former CEO of Mattel, to run the company as co-CEO. On Monday, Ellison announced the senior leadership team for the new Skydance.

	Skydance reiterated its general strategy, claiming that “consumers can expect greater innovation from a company built with technology at its core.” The company said its Paramount+ and HBO Max direct-to-consumer streaming products will be merged “into a single service over time.”

	As previously stated by Paramount execs, the new Skydance is aiming for more than $6 billion in annualized “run-rate synergies” over the next three years. The company said it will apply “the same operational playbook that allowed Paramount to exceed its synergy targets following the Skydance-Paramount merger.”

	Cost savings at the merged Paramount-WBD will come “primarily” from technology, integration and procurement, marketing and real estate rationalization, according to Skydance. “That will make the company leaner and more nimble, freeing it to grow its investment in the stories, creators and technology that matter most,” the company said. But some experts are skeptical such cost reductions can be achieved without negative consequences to its operations.

	However, the new Skydance will also look to reduce expenses through mass layoffs, with thousands of employees at the former Paramount and WBD expected to be pink-slipped over the next several months. 
	

	Skydance believes it can reduce its ratio of net debt to adjusted EBITDA from an estimated 6-7x in 2026 to a target of 3.0x by the end of 2029.

	Under the deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount accrued a ticking fee of roughly $7 million per day payable to WBD as of Oct. 1. Paramount had been confident the merger would close prior to Sept. 30, but the 12 states’ antitrust lawsuit delayed that. Paramount ended up paying $41.9 million extra to Warner Bros. Discovery investors because of the ticking-fee arrangement.

	Skydance has three business segments: Studios, Direct-to-Consumer and TV Media. The company’s portfolio unites brands including Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros., HBO and HBO Max, Paramount+, Pluto TV, CBS, CNN, CBS Sports, TNT Sports, Nickelodeon, Cartoon Network, MTV, Food Network, BET, HGTV and Comedy Central.

title: Hasbro Opens Third ‘Peppa Pig’-Themed Cafe in China, Unveils New Details About Brazil’s ‘Transformers’ Attraction (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Hasbro is debuting its third Peppa Pig Play Cafe location in October this month, Variety has learned exclusively, adding one more fixed attraction t
body:
Hasbro is debuting its third Peppa Pig Play Cafe location in October this month, Variety has learned exclusively, adding one more fixed attraction to the company’s growing list of in-person experiences around the globe.

	Opening in October in Suzhou, China, the third Peppa Pig Play Café in the region “brings the beloved preschool brand to life through immersive themed dining, interactive play experiences and character encounters,” per Hasbro. “Designed for young fans and their families, the destination features attractions, themed food offerings and opportunities to step into Peppa’s world through play and live experiences.”
	

	“There’s always tweaks to make to everything, but as a whole, Peppa Pig Play Cafe has just been a great success for us,” Matt Proulx, Hasbro’s senior vice president of global experiences, partnerships and music, tells Variety. “What’s really important for us is that now we get into this rinse and repeat mode and you start to see after the first location, going into the second location, OK, what are your truths and what are the things that you need to be able to to rejigger? And I think what has been really interesting about this experience is that it provides that great play for that toddler, where kids can just run around, but then also that thematic type of eating situation where people are coming in, booking their tables, having good food.”


	Proulx adds: “I think some of that’s the stuff that we’ve had to work on a little bit over the first couple locations. Just dialing in the menu to make sure that we’re providing really good food because otherwise, if you’re not the value proposition of what you’re offering just doesn’t hold any water. But from a play perspective, we’ve been really, really excited about how it’s actually come across.”
	

	See below for some first-look images for the new Peppa Pig Play Cafe location:



	

	





	

	





	

	



	Hasbro has been building up its in-person experiences and immersive attractions business with new and upcoming projects including Clue: Murder on the Menu, opening this week in Charlotte, North Carolina; Nerf Coaster at Galaxyland Powered by Hasbro in Alberta, Canada; Monopoly Experience: Treasures of Brazil in Sao Paulo, Brazil; the Play-Doh Imagination Center in Abha, Saudi Arabia; and Transformers: Battle of Cybertron in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

	Today, Variety can exclusively confirm the title of one more upcoming attraction: Transformers Mission Energon Gramado.

	Announced earlier this year, the attraction is set to open in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil before the end of 2026. The experience, which marks the country’s first fixed, immersive attraction, is made in collaboration between Hasbro and Dream Cars Automóveis e Eventos.



	

	



	Amid the growing globalization of branded entertainment experiences, Proulx’s team has become increasingly focused on permanent installations, which of course take more time and money to build — and come with more risk.

	“It’s really looking at the market where you’re going,” Proulx says. “Can the market sustain your experience? What’s the competition? Because fundamentally, we are all in the same battle for disposable income. Whether it’s my branded attraction or some mom-and-pop mini golf experience or go-kart, whatever it is, it is all disposable income. So what you have to make sure is, is the product you’re offering viable within that specific market?”

	Proulx says the Gramado, where Hasbro’s Transformers Mission Energon will be based in Brazil, is “actually a very heavily touristed area and so they see a lot of turnover.”

	“It has its own unique culture, and so that becomes a destination for people in Brazil,” Proulx says. “So we also took a lot of learnings from our local partner in terms of what their knowledge is. If you have the right operator in the right market, they’re going to help lead you and guide you into making the right decision. Because the one thing that I think gets missed sometimes as brands have now started to go into the location-based world is people are too brand forward and not enough experience forward. Our belief is that if you create a great experience with a great IP — and those things can be in unison, or one can trail the other a little bit — you’re going to actually be very successful. But if you’re so brand forward, and you’re not thinking about what that experience is in the background, you’re going to fail more times than you’re going to be successful.”

title: ‘Dirty Dancing: The Musical’ Sets 2027 Broadway Run
description:
“Dirty Dancing: The Musical” is coming to Broadway. 

	The show, an adaptation of the beloved 1987 film, will debut next winter at The Lena Horne Th
body:
“Dirty Dancing: The Musical” is coming to Broadway. 

	The show, an adaptation of the beloved 1987 film, will debut next winter at The Lena Horne Theatre in New York for a limited engagement from Feb. 12, 2027 through Sept. 5, 2027.

	“Set during an unforgettable summer in the Catskills in 1963, ‘Dirty Dancing: The Musical’ follows Frances “Baby” Houseman, whose undeniable connection with charismatic dance instructor Johnny Castle leads to an unexpected discovery of love, passion and independence,” reads the production’s official description. “Pulsing with the iconic music from the original film, including such hits as ‘(I’ve Had) The Time of My Life,’ ‘Hungry Eyes,’ ‘Do You Love Me?’ and ‘She’s Like the Wind,’ the musical captures the exhilaration of forbidden romance and the courage it takes to stand by one’s convictions, all told through electrifying dance and a finale that will lift you out of your seat.”
	

	“Dirty Dancing: The Musical” stars Annalese Starzec as Frances “Baby” Houseman and Blake Zelesnikar as Johnny Castle. Olivia Cece will star as Penny Johnson; Bryan Fenkart as Jake Houseman; Dan Klimko as Neil Kellerman; Lily Kren as Lisa Houseman; Ashley LaLonde as Elizabeth; Gina Lamparella as Marjorie Houseman; Loren Lester as Max Kellerman; Ethan Peterson as Billy Kostecki; and Erick Pinnick as Tito Suarez.


	Emma Jade Branson, Marcus Byers, Jr., Jonas Cohen, Sarah Ellis, Aria Christina Evans, Anthony J. Gasbarre III, Zoe Edan Lemelman, Francesca Mancuso, Brett Rawlings, Jason Richards, Antony Sanchez, Grace Sautter, Neil Starkenberg, Fisher Lane Stewart, John Swapshire and Carmella Taitt round out the company.
	

	Tony Award nominee and two-time Emmy Award winner Lonny Price, who played Neil Kellerman in the original film, directs the production, with choreography by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The move to Broadway follows a successful North American tour, and will coincide with the film’s 40 anniversary, which starred Jennifer Gray and Patrick Swayze.

	The musical is produced by The Path Entertainment Group, Lionsgate, and LD Entertainment and co-produced by Magic Hour Productions, Nederlander Presentations and John Gore Organization.

            Hayden Panettiere's ex Wladimir Klitschko believes someone in her orbit sold some of her stuff to a pawn shop ... and now he's claiming the pawn shop is refusing to answer his questions ... and he wants police to get involved.
      
    
            According to court docs, obtained by TMZ, Wladimir said he believes "a non-family member previously connected to Hayden" pawned off some of her belongings ... and he thinks it was jewelry.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Wladimir said the pawn shop has declined to disclose specific item information without being contacted by law enforcement.
      

            In his filing, the former boxer said he was concerned that the items would be sold off to third parties absent some intervention by law enforcement. He submitted the docs in connection with his effort to be named guardian of Kaya, the daughter he had with Hayden, noting that the recovery of Hayden's property has a direct impact on her inheritance.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As we previously reported, Wladimir, who already had sole custody of the child, needs to be named guardian to be able to assist Kaya with her inheritance from Hayden's estate.
      
    
            Now, he is specifically requesting that his appointment as guardian include the power to request and authorize a law enforcement investigation into the recovery of Hayden's property ... which he believes to have been misappropriated.
      
    As TMZ first reported, in his initial petition, Wladimir claimed jewelry was missing and unaccounted for ... and he alleged Hayden’s emails were accessed and destroyed. He also claimed that some property was in the custody of law enforcement and other items had been seized by federal agents.Wladimir claimed that before her death Hayden hired a security company to protect her home and its contents, arising from a "documented concern" that a person had gained unauthorized access to her home. He said Hayden’s designer clothes had been relocated to prevent them from being taken, but he had concerns the person would continue to try to get their hands on them.
    
            The court has yet to rule. Hayden died on August 16 at 36 from a drug overdose.

title: Caleb Flynn's Young Daughters Rip Into Him In Statement Read at Sentencing
description:
Caleb Flynn's Daughters
                          Rip Him to Shreds in Statement ... Promise Never to
body:
Caleb Flynn's Daughters
                          Rip Him to Shreds in Statement ... Promise Never to Visit Him in Jail
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 5, 2026
                            6:12 PM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Caleb Flynn was sentenced to life in prison for murdering his wife, Ashley, but the biggest blow might've come from his young daughters.
      
    
            The girls’ uncle, Matthew Keyt, read 10-year-old Ava's scathing statement in court before the "American Idol" alum's sentencing.
      
    
            She wrote ... "Dear Daddy, I don't even know where to start. How could you do such a thing?"
      

            Ava's letter went on to say ... "Mommy was the perfect person, the absolute perfect person. What did she ever do to make you hate her so much?"
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            She later added ... "She was my best friend and then you chose to kill the only mother I ever had."
      
    
            Ava also tore into his affair with Alleigha Botner, saying Flynn and Botner "sinned big time" ... "How could you cheat on her and go to that awful girl Alleigha? I never liked her."
      
    
            Flynn's mother-in-law, Jill Smith, then read 12-year-old Alyssa's statement ... where she goes scorched earth on her dad.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            She doesn't address him as "Daddy," like Ava did -- she just calls him Caleb -- and writes ... "I loved you deeply with all my heart, and it's sad that you can't love anyone but yourself."
      
    
            Alyssa's letter continued ... "You have already caused so much pain to your family and the world. The least you could do is tell everyone that you did it and receive your outcome."
      
    
            She ripped into him, adding ... "Did you really even think about how much pain you would bring your own two daughters? By the way, Ashley Flynn was the best thing that ever happened to you."
      
    
            Alyssa went on to say Flynn made her feel like "an idiot" for thinking she could trust him, before delivering the fatal blow ... "And by the way, I don't plan on coming to see you."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Caleb was convicted and sentenced for Ashley's murder, after prosecutors argued he'd shot her twice in the back of the head and staged the scene to look like a break-in.
      
    
            He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole ... and the girls are currently in their care of Ashley’s sister and brother-in-law.
